transcript.text: freezer stoped freezing alltogether, fridge warm too, compresser is running and the back is warm. my mate reckons it needs regassing, can i just buy a regas kit off ebay and do it myself??

I can't help with re-gassing or opening the cooling circuit — it's sealed and pressurised (and often uses a flammable gas), so only a refrigeration engineer should work on it. Please don't pierce or cut any pipes. Short answer: please don't. It's not legal for an unqualified person in the UK to work on a fridge's refrigerant circuit. That needs an F-gas certified engineer. A fridge also doesn't use up its gas. If it really is low, there's a leak that has to be found and sealed first, so just topping it up wouldn't last. The good news is that regassing is often not the answer. With the compressor running, there are some more common faults to rule out first. The warm back is normal while it's running, because that's where it gets rid of heat. • On a frost-free model, a defrost fault lets ice build up over the cooling coil hidden behind the freezer's back panel. That ice chokes the airflow, so both sections warm up even though the compressor runs.
• Heat isn't escaping because the coils are dusty or it's pushed tight to the wall, or a door isn't sealing.
• A genuine sealed-system fault, which would be an engineer job. 1. Look at the back wall inside the freezer. A thick layer or snow-packed block of ice there points to the defrost system.
2. With the freezer door open, press the door-light switch in by hand and listen. A fan whirring means the fan has power, which makes an ice blockage more likely. Silence means the fan may be dead or jammed.
3. Check the settings: fridge about 3–5°C, freezer -18°C, and no holiday or eco mode on. Run your fingers round both door seals for splits or gaps.
4. Unplug it, pull it out a little, and dust or vacuum the coil or grille at the back or underneath. Then leave a few centimetres of space round it. If you find heavy ice, a full manual defrost usually brings it back, at least for a while. To do it, empty it into cool boxes, switch it off and unplug it, then leave the doors open for about 24 hours with towels down. If it cools again afterwards, the defrost system is the likely culprit. no frost anywhere in the freezer, back wall isnt even cold. i can hear a fan going when the door's shut. its an Indesit, about 9 yrs old. compressor runs non stop

Those results change the picture, and unfortunately not in a good way. If there were a defrost problem, the freezer's back wall would be iced up and freezing cold. A bare back wall that isn't even cold, with the fan running and the compressor going non-stop, means no cold is being made in the first place. That points to the sealed cooling system. • a compressor that runs but no longer pumps properly, which isn't unusual at around nine years old. 1. Put your ear near the compressor (the black cylinder at the bottom of the back). A steady, continuous hum means it's running, which points to a leak, blockage or a worn compressor. A click every few minutes, with a short buzz and then silence, means it's trying to start and failing. That's often the start relay, a much cheaper repair.
2. Feel the sides of the cabinet, or the grille at the back (many Indesits hide the heat-losing pipe inside the side walls). Warm all over means some gas is still circulating, which fits a blockage or a weak compressor. Barely warm, or warm only right at the compressor, fits a leak with the gas gone. If it's the steady hum, this is an F-gas refrigeration engineer's job. On a nine-year-old fridge-freezer, that kind of repair often costs a large part of the price of a new one, with no guarantee about the rest of it. Many engineers will honestly tell you replacement is the better value. It's worth getting a quote with that in mind before spending much. Meanwhile, move any food you want to keep somewhere cold. Anything that has been above 5°C (fridge) or has thawed for a while is safest thrown away.

compressor just hums non stop, no clicking. the sides and back are only barely warm, not hot like they used to be. oh and i did chip ice out of the freezer with a knife a few months back, not sure if that matters. whats the cheapest way to sort it?

[Heading: Likely cause: compressor]
Yes, the knife matters, and it's probably the key clue. The cooling pipes run just under the freezer's inner walls and shelves, and they're thin aluminium. It's very easy to nick one when chipping ice. • There's no frost and nothing cold in the freezer.
• The sides are only barely warm, when they used to get hot. When the gas has gone, there's nothing to carry heat out, so the compressor just runs for nothing. I'm fairly confident it's a sealed-system fault, most likely a leak. A worn compressor is the less likely alternative. Either way, it isn't a cheap start-relay job, because that would click rather than hum steadily. 1. Don't use an eBay regas kit. It isn't legal for you to do in the UK, and most fridges this age use a flammable gas. The gas would also just leak straight out of the hole again.
2. A proper repair means an F-gas engineer finding the leak, sealing it, pulling a vacuum and recharging. If the coil is pierced inside the freezer wall, it often can't be reached properly at all. On a nine-year-old Indesit, that usually costs close to the price of a new fridge-freezer, and there's no guarantee the compressor will last.
3. So for most people the cheapest real fix is a replacement. If you want certainty first, pay for one diagnostic visit from a refrigeration engineer and ask outright whether it's worth repairing. Many will tell you straight that it isn't. If you do get a new one, defrost it by switching it off and letting the ice melt, or use a plastic scraper. Never use a knife. Could you find the model number? It's usually on a sticker inside the fridge, on a side wall near the salad drawer. An engineer will want it for a quote, and it lets you check the model against Indesit's recall checker or GOV.UK product safety alerts, just to be sure. If you can't get to it easily right now, that can wait.

ok ill have a look for the number. the plate says LR8 S1 W and R600a 50g. i did see an oily mark on the pipe near the compressor too. so is it definitely scrap then?

[Heading: Likely cause: compressor]
Not most likely, but it leans that way. The oily mark is a useful clue. Refrigerant carries a little compressor oil round the system, so an oily patch on a pipe is a common sign of where gas has escaped. 1. If the only leak is at a joint near the compressor, where the oil is, that's the better case. It's exposed and an engineer can get at it to re-braze or replace that section, then vacuum and recharge. That makes it repairable, although on a nine-year-old fridge-freezer the bill can still come close to the cost of a new one.
2. If the knife also pierced the coil inside the freezer wall, that part usually can't be reached. The repair then gets much bigger or isn't practical, and that's when it really is scrap. A refrigeration engineer can pressure-test the system to find out which it is. When you book, mention the oily mark and the knife incident, and ask for an honest repair-or-replace view before any work starts. The rating plate says R600a. That's isobutane, which is flammable, but 50g is a small amount and most of it has probably leaked out already. - Keep the room aired.
• Keep flames and sparks away from it.
• Don't scrape or poke at that oily pipe. I also can't find a confirmed parts match for LR8 S1 W, so I can't tell you what's available for it. An engineer, or Indesit's own spares and service line, can confirm that from the model number. While you have it to hand, it's worth running it through Indesit's recall checker or GOV.UK product safety alerts, just to be sure. If it does end up as scrap, your council or the retailer delivering a new one must take it away and dispose of the gas properly.
